nameStory: Pickerelweed gets its name from its association with pickerel fish, which lurk among these aquatic plants in shallow waters. The heart-shaped leaves and dense growth provide perfect cover for these predatory fish as they hunt for smaller prey in ponds and lake edges.
description: Pickerelweed is a sturdy aquatic plant that grows along the edges of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. This water-loving perennial produces distinctive heart-shaped leaves that emerge directly from the water on thick, spongy stems. In summer, it sends up beautiful spikes of small blue-purple flowers that create a striking display above the water surface. The plant typically grows 1-4 feet tall, forming dense colonies that provide important habitat for fish, frogs, and waterfowl.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with smooth edges and prominent parallel veins running from base to tip. Feel thick and slightly waxy, emerging singly on long, spongy stems directly from underwater roots.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense spikes of small blue to purple flowers clustered at the top of tall stems. Each tiny flower has six petals with one petal marked by two yellow spots that act like landing strips for pollinators.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in shallow water or soggy soil at water's edge, with stems rising directly from creeping underwater rhizomes. Forms dense colonies that can cover large areas of shoreline.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, hollow, and spongy-feeling stems that feel almost inflated when squeezed gently. This air-filled tissue helps the plant float and get oxygen to underwater parts.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, hard, ridged seeds develop in late summer within the dried flower spike. Seeds are important food for ducks and other waterfowl.

habitat: Look for pickerelweed in shallow water along the edges of ponds, lakes, marshes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It thrives in muddy or sandy bottoms in water depths from just a few inches to about 3 feet deep. Often grows alongside cattails, arrowhead, and water lilies in these wetland communities.

seasonality.spring: New heart-shaped leaves emerge from underwater rhizomes in late spring, unfurling as water temperatures warm. Early leaves may be partially submerged before reaching full height.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with full-sized heart-shaped leaves and showy blue-purple flower spikes blooming from June through August. Flowers are most vibrant in early morning.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back, while seed heads persist and provide food for waterfowl. Seeds ripen and fall, often floating to new locations.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underwater rhizomes. Only dried, brown stems and seed heads may remain poking above ice in shallow areas.

funFact: Pickerelweed flowers are "explosive" pollinators - when a bee lands on the yellow spots, the flower literally shoots pollen onto the visitor's back with a tiny spring-loaded mechanism, ensuring the bee carries pollen to the next flower even if it doesn't want to!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with arrowhead (Sagittaria species), but arrowhead has distinctly arrow-shaped leaves with pointed lobes, while pickerelweed leaves are heart-shaped with rounded lobes. Memory trick: "Pickerel hearts" vs "Sagittarius arrows."
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the pickerel name with the fish, this plant actually benefits many fish species beyond pickerel, serving as a crucial nursery habitat for bass, bluegill, and other freshwater fish. The dense underwater root systems help prevent shoreline erosion.
compareHints: Pickerelweed differs from its tropical relative, common water hyacinth, by growing rooted in mud rather than floating freely. Water hyacinth has inflated leaf stems and much showier purple flowers, while pickerelweed has solid heart-shaped leaves on spongy stems. Water hyacinth is considered invasive in warmer climates but rarely survives New England winters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its genus relative pickerelweed, water hyacinth is free-floating with inflated leaf stems and rounded leaves, while pickerelweed is rooted with heart-shaped leaves.
